result: They characterize the most probable paths and invariant sets associated with noise-induced transitions to turbulence.
conclusion: The work provides insight into the role of noise in triggering turbulence transitions, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Current-induced Successive Structural Phase Transitions Beyond Thermal Equilibrium In Single-crystal ${\mathrm{VO}}_{2}$
authors: Shunsuke Kitou, Akitoshi Nakano, Masato Imaizumi, Yuiga Nakamura, Yuto Nakamura, Hideo Kishida, Taka-Hisa Arima, And Ichiro Terasaki
abstract:
Author(s): Shunsuke Kitou, Akitoshi Nakano, Masato Imaizumi, Yuiga Nakamura, Yuto Nakamura, Hideo Kishida, Taka-hisa Arima, and Ichiro Terasaki

Using synchrotron x-ray diffraction, optical microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy, current-induced structural phase transitions in single-crystal vanadium dioxide are investigated. Successive transitions to two distinct metallic tetragonal phases are observed, including a nonequilibrium structure with isotropic lattice expansion inaccessible under thermal equilibrium.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022050] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports current-induced structural phase transitions in VO2 single crystals, revealing nonequilibrium metallic phases not accessible under thermal equilibrium.
motivation: To understand how electric currents can drive structural phase transitions beyond thermal equilibrium, potentially enabling new pathways to control material properties.
method: Combined synchrotron x-ray diffraction, optical microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy to characterize structural changes in single-crystal VO2 under applied current.
result: Observation of successive transitions to two distinct metallic tetragonal phases, including a nonequilibrium structure with isotropic lattice expansion.
conclusion: Current-induced effects can produce structural phases inaccessible by heating alone, highlighting the role of non-thermal pathways in phase transitions.

title: Dynamical Learning In Deep Asymmetric Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Davide Badalotti, Carlo Baldassi, Marc Mézard, Mattia Scardecchia, And Riccardo Zecchina
abstract:
Author(s): Davide Badalotti, Carlo Baldassi, Marc Mézard, Mattia Scardecchia, and Riccardo Zecchina

We investigate recurrent neural networks with asymmetric interactions and demonstrate that the inclusion of self-couplings or sparse excitatory intermodule connections leads to the emergence of a densely connected manifold of dynamically accessible stable configurations. This representation manifold…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023281] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical learning in asymmetric recurrent neural networks, focusing on the emergence of stable configuration manifolds.
motivation: To understand how asymmetric interactions and self-couplings in recurrent neural networks can lead to complex dynamical behavior and learning.
method: The authors analyze recurrent neural networks with asymmetric interactions, incorporating self-couplings or sparse excitatory intermodule connections, and study the resulting dynamical properties.
result: They find that such networks develop a densely connected manifold of dynamically accessible stable configurations, which can serve as a representation manifold.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the dynamics and learning capabilities of asymmetric recurrent neural networks, with potential implications for machine learning.

title: Trapping And Cooling Mechanisms In Blue-detuned Magneto-optical Traps Of Molecules
authors: Qinshu Lyu And M. R. Tarbutt
abstract:
Author(s): Qinshu Lyu and M. R. Tarbutt

This work identifies the mechanisms responsible for trapping and cooling in a blue-detuned magneto-optical trap driven by a pair of closely spaced frequency components of opposite circular polarization. When the Zeeman splitting matches the frequency difference between the two components, there is a state that is dark to the beam propagating in one direction but not to the beam from the opposite direction, generating a radiation pressure force toward the field zero.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023259] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies trapping and cooling mechanisms in blue-detuned magneto-optical traps for molecules, focusing on a specific laser configuration and Zeeman splitting.
motivation: To understand and improve the trapping and cooling of molecules using blue-detuned magneto-optical traps, which is important for molecular physics and ultracold chemistry.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a blue-detuned MOT driven by two closely spaced frequency components with opposite circular polarization, identifying a dark state mechanism that generates a radiation pressure force toward the field zero.
result: They identify that when Zeeman splitting matches the frequency difference, a state is dark to one beam but not the opposite, producing a trapping force. The mechanisms for cooling and trapping are explained.
conclusion: The work provides a clear understanding of the trapping and cooling mechanisms in this type of MOT, which can guide experimental implementations for molecules.

title: Three-Dimensional Xy Universality And Nonlinear Magnetic Susceptibility In A Kagome Ice Compound
authors: Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, And Philipp Gegenwart
abstract:
Author(s): Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, and Philipp Gegenwart

Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe reveal hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground states, reached via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021043] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in a kagome spin ice compound, revealing hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.
motivation: To investigate the nature of the ground state and phase transition in the kagome ice compound HoAgGe, which exhibits spin ice behavior and potential hidden order.
method: The authors performed nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements and analyzed critical exponents to identify the universality class of the transition.
result: They found evidence of hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground state, with the transition belonging to the three-dimensional XY universality class.
conclusion: The study provides insight into the exotic magnetic phases of kagome ice systems and the role of symmetry breaking.

title: Robust Orbital-Selective Flat Bands In Layered Transition-Metal Oxyhalides At Room Temperature
authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin
abstract:
Author(s): Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, and Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021041] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the discovery of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides at room temperature, characterized by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but many are only stable at low temperatures. The authors aim to find a room-temperature stable platform.
method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to measure the electronic band structure.
result: They observe intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, with orbital selectivity.
conclusion: These materials provide a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states at ambient conditions.

title: Intertwined Polar, Chiral, And Ferro-Rotational Orders In A Homo-Ferro-Rotational Insulator
authors: Weizhe Zhang, June Ho Yeo, Xiaoyu Guo, Tony Chiang, Nishkarsh Agarwal, John T. Heron, Kai Sun, Junjie Yang, Sang-Wook Cheong, Youngjun Ahn, And Liuyan Zhao
abstract:
Author(s): Weizhe Zhang, June Ho Yeo, Xiaoyu Guo, Tony Chiang, Nishkarsh Agarwal, John T. Heron, Kai Sun, Junjie Yang, Sang-Wook Cheong, Youngjun Ahn, and Liuyan Zhao

Multimodal optical characterization of Ni
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021030] Published Fri May 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of intertwined polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational orders in a homo-ferro-rotational insulator using multimodal optical characterization.
motivation: To understand the coupling between different ferroic orders and the formation of complex domain walls in materials with ferro-rotational order.
method: Multimodal optical characterization techniques (e.g., second harmonic generation, optical anisotropy) were used to probe the polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational domains in Ni2Mo3O8.
result: A uniform ferro-rotational state was identified that couples polarity and chirality, leading to complex mixed-type domain walls.
conclusion: The findings reveal a new type of multiferroic order with intertwined ferroic properties, which may have implications for fundamental physics and potential applications.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: A review of radiation forces and torques in optics and acoustics, focusing on wave-matter interactions and particle manipulation.
motivation: To provide a unified perspective on how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in wave fields induce forces and torques on particles, with applications in trapping, sorting, and pulling.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks and experimental demonstrations of optical and acoustic forces and torques, emphasizing common principles.
result: It highlights that both optical and acoustic fields can exert forces and torques via similar mechanisms, enabling diverse applications like nanoparticle trapping and cell sorting.
conclusion: The review underscores the rich physics and practical potential of wave-induced forces and torques, but does not directly contribute to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements
authors: Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, And Thomas E. Albrecht
abstract:
Author(s): Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, and Thomas E. Albrecht

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of the physics and chemistry of transplutonium elements under high pressure, focusing on their electronic properties and material behavior.
motivation: Transplutonium elements are important for nuclear applications and exhibit unique electronic behavior due to 5f electrons at the boundary of localization and itinerancy.
method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical studies of metals, alloys, compounds, and coordination complexes under high pressure.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of how pressure affects the electronic structure, bonding, and phase transitions in transplutonium materials.
conclusion: High-pressure studies reveal complex behavior in transplutonium materials, but the field remains challenging due to radioactivity and electronic complexity.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete defect picture.
result: The review highlights how these techniques can directly access atomic-scale disorder information in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space probes provides a more comprehensive understanding of defects in semiconductors.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on collective motion in biological and soft matter systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors, with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active systems, presenting a unified mathematical framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, distinct from neighbor-based alignment.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental mechanism in active matter that opens new avenues for designing smart materials and understanding biological motion.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory effects in soft amorphous materials, specifically in biopolymer networks like collagen, which are important for biological tissues.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks under nonlinear strain-stiffening conditions.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory effect) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials, with implications for biological tissue mechanics.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental demonstrations of continuous thermochemical sources for producing AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors use a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal to produce AlF, and characterize the molecular beam using spectroscopy and buffer gas cooling.
result: They achieve a compact oven with high brightness, continuous output exceeding pulsed sources, and demonstrate rotational cooling to ~30 K using a cryogenic buffer gas cell.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can enable direct loading of magneto-optical traps, advancing molecular quantum science.

title: Analytical Response Functions For A Compressible Thin Fluid Layer With Odd Viscosity *
authors: Yuto Hosaka And Shigeyuki Komura Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider
abstract: Fluids composed of chiral active components can exhibit odd viscosity, a property that breaks time-reversal and parity symmetries. We investigate the hydrodynamic response to monopole and dipole singularities in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, supported by a conventional lubrication layer. Using the two-dimensional Green’s function in Fourier space, we derive analytical solutions for the flow and pressure fields. These solutions provide a detailed description of the hydrodynamic interactions governing the motion of colloidal particles and microswimmers in confined chiral fluids, offering insight into the role of odd viscosity in modifying particle dynamics and collective behavior. The derived results are directly applicable to modeling transport, control, and self-organization phenomena in active and chiral microfluidic systems.
tldr: This paper studies hydrodynamic response functions in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, focusing on chiral active fluids.
motivation: Odd viscosity arises in chiral active fluids and affects particle dynamics and collective behavior; understanding its hydrodynamic effects is important for microfluidic applications.
method: The authors use two-dimensional Green's functions in Fourier space to derive analytical solutions for flow and pressure fields induced by monopole and dipole singularities.
result: Analytical expressions for the flow and pressure fields are obtained, showing how odd viscosity modifies hydrodynamic interactions.
conclusion: The results provide a framework for modeling transport and self-organization in chiral microfluidic systems.

title: Electromagnetic Characterization Of Magnetic Ring: Case Of Circular Cross-Section Shape
authors: Lars Sj\"oberg Taha El Hajji
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive two-dimensional analytical model of a toroidal magnetic ring with circular cross-section under sinusoidal excitation. Applying Maxwell's equations in local polar coordinates within a complex permeability, the model derives analytical expressions for the internal magnetic field, magnetic flux, complex impedance, and total losses. It rigorously separates the contributions of eddy current losses, hysteresis losses, and winding losses, while explicitly incorporating the skin effect in the conductive core via Bessel functions. An expression for the apparent permeability is also provided, enabling the nonlinear core behavior to be mapped onto simplified linear material models. The resulting analytical model offers a computationally efficient and accurate foundation for standardized magnetic material characterization, such as Brockhaus and Iwatsu ring measurements, as a powerful alternative to 2D and 3D finite element analysis.
tldr: This paper presents an analytical model for the electromagnetic characterization of a toroidal magnetic ring with circular cross-section, focusing on eddy current and hysteresis losses.
motivation: To provide a computationally efficient alternative to finite element analysis for standardized magnetic material characterization.
method: Maxwell's equations are solved in local polar coordinates with complex permeability, incorporating skin effect via Bessel functions.
result: Analytical expressions for internal magnetic field, flux, impedance, and losses are derived, including apparent permeability.
conclusion: The model offers an accurate and efficient tool for magnetic ring characterization, replacing 2D/3D FEM.

title: Design And Performance Of A Heated Gas Injector For Producing Cold Molecular Beams
authors: Avneesh Verma, Jack Mango, Shungo Fukaya, Arian Jadbabaie, Sepehr Ebadi, Ronald F. Garcia Ruiz, John M. Doyle
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We realize an injector device that supplies warm gas directly into a cryogenic environment. This injector has several advantageous features, including robustness, rigidity, simple installation, and excellent thermal isolation between a hot ([MATH]300 K) copper fill line and a cold ([MATH]3 K) cryogenic buffer gas cell. Less than 200 mW heat load on the cell is observed in realistic conditions of a molecular precision measurement experiment. A polyamide-imide (PAI) tube is the essential design feature. The fill line is epoxied to one end of the tube while the other end of the tube is connected to the cell via a slip-fit onto a brass nipple, realizing a complete vacuum-tight seal. PAI contracts on the brass nipple when cooled, forming a cryogenic leak-tight seal. The injector is easily (de-)mountable and rigid, with no significant displacement of the fill line relative to the cell observed during cooldown to 4 K. We characterize injector performance by flowing into the cell [MATH] through the hot fill line and cold [MATH] buffer gas through a separate cryogenic fill line while laser ablating a barium-containing target. This produces cold BaF free radicals, detected using absorption spectroscopy. This injector design will be employed to laser cool radium-containing molecules, such as [MATH] and [MATH], where leak-tight delivery of [MATH] and [MATH] reagents into a cryogenic buffer gas cell is required for scientific and safety reasons. These molecules are of particular interest for the study of symmetry-violating nuclear properties and searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.
tldr: This paper describes the design and performance of a heated gas injector for producing cold molecular beams, focusing on engineering aspects for precision measurement experiments.
motivation: To enable leak-tight delivery of reactive gases into a cryogenic buffer gas cell for producing cold molecules, which are used in searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.
method: The injector uses a polyamide-imide (PAI) tube to thermally isolate a hot fill line from a cold cell, with a slip-fit seal that becomes leak-tight upon cooling. Performance is characterized by flowing gas and laser ablation to produce BaF molecules, detected via absorption spectroscopy.
result: The injector achieves less than 200 mW heat load on the cell, is rigid and easy to mount, and maintains a vacuum-tight seal during cooldown to 4 K.
conclusion: The injector design is robust and suitable for delivering reactive chemicals for cold molecule production in precision measurement experiments.

title: Exact Propagating Dirac Wave Packets In An Attractive Coulomb-like Potential
authors: Siddhant Das
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct exact, positive-energy, normalizable wave-packet solutions of the Dirac equation in the axisymmetric potential [MATH] -- to our knowledge, the first such solutions in any external potential. Remarkably, one family comprises only elementary functions whose longitudinal profiles reproduce the free-Schr\"odinger Hermite--Gauss wave packets in the nonrelativistic limit. All packets share two striking features: (i) a probability density that is pointwise decoupled from spin orientation -- despite the inherent spin-orbit coupling of the Dirac equation -- and (ii) a complete freezing of their time evolution at the critical coupling [MATH]. We also present a simple scheme that maps solutions of the 2D Helmholtz equation to further exact Dirac wave packets.
tldr: Constructs exact Dirac wave packets in an attractive Coulomb-like potential, with decoupled probability density and frozen evolution at critical coupling.
motivation: To find exact, normalizable wave-packet solutions of the Dirac equation in an external potential, which are rare and important for understanding relativistic quantum dynamics.
method: Analytical construction using separation of variables and mapping to 2D Helmholtz equation; solutions expressed in terms of elementary functions and special functions.
result: Obtained two families of exact wave packets with pointwise spin-independent probability density and complete freezing of time evolution at a critical coupling strength.
conclusion: These exact solutions provide a new tool for studying relativistic quantum mechanics and may have implications for quantum information or thermodynamics, but the paper does not address those connections.

title: Deep Research In Physical Sciences: A Multi-Agent Framework And Comprehensive Benchmark
authors: Yigeng Jiang, Tengchao Yang, Taoyong Cui, Jiaxing Wan, Yuan Wang, Weida Wang, Zhiyu Liu, Chuyi Peng, Binzhao Luo, Maoli Gao, Huaihai Huang, Yuqianer Zeng, Ziyang Zheng, Dongchen Huang, Chao Chen, Zichao Liu, Weiping Shen, Shuchen Pu, Siyu Zhou, Runmin Ma, Yusong Hu, Fei Chao, Bo Zhang, Xiawu Zheng, Zifu Wang, Lei Bai, Yunqi Cai, Shufei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep research agents are Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems designed for autonomous, multi-step scientific reasoning, and they hold immense potential for accelerating research in the physical sciences. However, comprehensive and in-depth evaluations of their capabilities within this domain remain lacking. To address this gap, we introduce PhySciBench, a benchmark highly relevant to physical science research, comprising 200 expert-curated questions, balanced between physics and chemistry, across six task categories that reflect real-world scientific workflows. Evaluations of state-of-the-art models and agent systems on PhySciBench reveal limited performance; even the strongest baseline, Gemini Deep Research, achieves an accuracy of only 33.5%. Analysis of failure cases identifies three recurrent deficiencies: fragility in extended reasoning chains, limited knowledge transfer across steps, and a lack of physics-grounded self-verification. Motivated by these findings, we develop DelveAgent, a modular multi-agent framework equipped with an adaptive planning loop, dual-granularity memory, and a hierarchical physics-grounded reflection mechanism. Across four scientific benchmarks, DelveAgent improves accuracy by up to 7.5 percentage points while reducing inference costs to approximately one-third of the strongest baseline. These results establish the significance of PhySciBench as a critical benchmark for evaluating AI systems in the physical sciences and demonstrate that architectural specialization can effectively enhance the reliability of autonomous scientific research.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark and multi-agent framework for evaluating LLM-based research agents in physical sciences, with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: There is a lack of comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating AI systems in physical science research, and existing models show limited performance.
method: The authors create PhySciBench with 200 expert-curated questions and develop DelveAgent, a modular multi-agent framework with adaptive planning, dual-granularity memory, and physics-grounded reflection.
result: DelveAgent improves accuracy by up to 7.5 percentage points over baselines while reducing inference costs to about one-third.
conclusion: PhySciBench is a critical benchmark for AI in physical sciences, and architectural specialization enhances autonomous research reliability.

title: Magnetic-polarization-dependent Spectroscopy Of Lanthanide-doped Anisotropic Crystals
authors: Zoe Liestmann, Luca Koldeweyh, Moritz Badtke, Sascha Kalusniak, Christian Kr\"ankel, Hiroki Tanaka
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate that absorption and emission spectra of trivalent lanthanide-doped anisotropic crystals can exhibit a significant magnetic-polarization dependence, which has been largely overlooked in spectroscopic studies to date. Focusing on the uniaxial laser host LiYF4 (YLF) doped with Yb3+, Tm3+, Er3+, and Ho3+, we measure magnetic-polarization-dependent absorption and emission spectra for transitions with strong magnetic-dipole (MD) contributions predicted by theory. Our results reveal that MD-induced spectral anisotropy, i.e., spectral differences for the same electric field orientation but for different magnetic field orientations, is present even in these well-established laser materials. A complete spectroscopic characterization of uniaxial crystals requires three polarizations, including the [MATH]-polarization, with both the electric field vector E and the magnetic field vector H perpendicular to the c-axis (E [MATH] c, H [MATH] c), in addition to the commonly used two polarizations [MATH] (E [MATH] c, H [MATH] c) and [MATH] (E [MATH] c, H [MATH] c). We further discuss the observed MD-induced spectral anisotropy and calculated MD branching ratios, the impact of the anisotropy on emission cross-section calculations, and the relevance of our results to other uniaxial and biaxial crystals.
tldr: This paper studies magnetic-polarization-dependent spectroscopy of lanthanide-doped anisotropic crystals, focusing on spectral anisotropy due to magnetic-dipole transitions.
motivation: To highlight that magnetic-polarization effects are often overlooked in spectroscopy of uniaxial crystals, and to demonstrate that three polarizations are needed for complete characterization.
method: Experimental absorption and emission spectra measurements on YLF crystals doped with Yb3+, Tm3+, Er3+, and Ho3+ under different magnetic field orientations.
result: Significant magnetic-polarization-dependent spectral differences are observed for transitions with strong magnetic-dipole contributions, confirming theoretical predictions.
conclusion: A complete spectroscopic characterization of uniaxial crystals requires three polarizations, including the π-polarization with both E and H perpendicular to the c-axis.

title: A Skew Polynomial Framework For Constructing Division Algebras And Linear Maximum Rank Distance Codes
authors: Susanne Pumpluen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct division algebras and linear maximum rank distance (MRD) matrix codes using skew polynomials over fields. The non-unital division algebras we obtain generalize several prominent constructions: Sheekey's twisted cyclic pre-semifields, i.e. the pre-semifields associated with Jha-Johnson semifields and the semifields associated with Albert's generalized twisted fields. Our linear MRD codes generalize the constructions of Lobillo, Santonastaso and Sheekey. We present criteria for these algebras to be division algebras, respectively, for when these codes have maximum rank, and compare isotopic division algebras that appear throughout recent and classical literature. We compute some of their invariants.
tldr: This paper constructs division algebras and linear maximum rank distance codes using skew polynomials over fields, generalizing known constructions.
motivation: To unify and extend constructions of division algebras and MRD codes, which have applications in coding theory and cryptography.
method: Uses skew polynomial rings over fields to define non-unital division algebras and linear MRD codes, providing criteria for division algebra and maximum rank.
result: Generalizes Sheekey's twisted cyclic pre-semifields and Lobillo et al.'s MRD codes; computes invariants and compares isotopic algebras.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified approach to constructing division algebras and MRD codes, with potential for further generalizations.

title: Inferential Models: The Power Of Auxiliary Variables For Reasoning With Scientific Uncertainty
authors: Chuanhai Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central challenge in scientific inference is to produce uncertainty assessments that are both situation-specific and frequency-calibrated. This article examines inferential models (IMs) as a framework for prior-free probabilistic reasoning with scientific uncertainty. The central IM idea is to view the auxiliary variables in a sampling model as the source of model-based uncertainty. R. A. Fisher's fiducial inference transfers auxiliary randomness to the parameter space before applying probability calculus; IMs instead predict the unobserved auxiliary value with calibrated predictive random sets (PRSs) and transfer the resulting plausibility statements only afterward. This change in order yields valid uncertainty assessments and clarifies the relations among Fisherian fiducial reasoning, Neymanian confidence theory, Dempster-Shafer belief functions, generalized fiducial inference, and IMs. By comparing IMs with objective-prior Bayesian inference, the article argues that E. T. Jaynes' logic-of-science ambition can be continued without forcing all scientific uncertainty into a precise prior distribution because calibrated imprecision is often essential. Finally, the article suggests that a differential-geometric theory of IMs may be within reach, offering a possible route to foundational questions traditionally framed in terms of the likelihood principle.
tldr: This paper presents inferential models as a framework for prior-free probabilistic reasoning, focusing on auxiliary variables and calibrated predictive random sets.
motivation: To address the challenge of producing uncertainty assessments that are both situation-specific and frequency-calibrated without relying on prior distributions.
method: The paper develops inferential models (IMs) by predicting unobserved auxiliary values with calibrated predictive random sets and transferring plausibility statements to the parameter space.
result: IMs provide valid uncertainty assessments and clarify relationships among Fisherian fiducial inference, Neymanian confidence theory, Dempster-Shafer belief functions, and generalized fiducial inference.
conclusion: The IM framework offers a way to continue Jaynes' logic-of-science ambition without forcing all uncertainty into precise priors, and suggests a potential differential-geometric theory.

title: A Spectral Based Coefficient Of Determination For The Fit Of An MA(q) Model
authors: Sebastian K\"uhnert Holger Dette
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a spectral based coefficient of determination to measure how well the spectral density of a stationary process is represented by the class of MA([MATH]) models. Using periodogram-based estimators, we establish asymptotic normality, derive tests for the MA([MATH]) hypothesis, and construct procedures for determining the smallest order [MATH] achieving a prescribed approximation quality.
tldr: This paper develops a spectral-based coefficient of determination for assessing how well an MA(q) model fits a stationary time series.
motivation: To measure the approximation quality of MA(q) models for stationary processes using spectral density.
method: Uses periodogram-based estimators and establishes asymptotic normality to derive tests and order selection procedures.
result: Provides a coefficient of determination and hypothesis tests for the MA(q) assumption.
conclusion: The proposed method enables data-driven selection of the MA order with a prescribed approximation quality.

title: Computing Resonances Of Perturbed Schr\"odinger Equations: Application To Reissner-Norsdtr\"om-de Sitter Black Holes
authors: Genevi\`eve Dusson Valentin Arrigoni (UMLP)
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a numerical method for computing resonances of one-dimensional Schr\"odinger equations perturbed by a compactly supported potential, via finding zeros of the Wronskian associated with Jost solutions of the reference equation, computed through the resolution of Cauchy problems. All resonances located in a given domain are found efficiently using a defeated Newton algorithm. A key ingredient of the method is the choice of reference potential for which Jost solutions are known, which removes spurious resonances often encountered numerically. We test this method on three types of reference potentials and perturbations thereof: P\"oschl-Teller potentials, exponentially decaying potentials, and potentials associated with Reissner-Nordstr\"omde Sitter black holes. In particular we study the impact of perturbations on the resonances, and the stability of small resonances under perturbation. As an illustration, we use the method to numerically study the strong cosmic censorship hypothesis.
tldr: A numerical method for computing resonances of perturbed Schrödinger equations, applied to black hole physics.
motivation: To efficiently compute resonances of one-dimensional Schrödinger equations with compactly supported perturbations, avoiding spurious resonances.
method: Uses a defeated Newton algorithm to find zeros of the Wronskian of Jost solutions, with a carefully chosen reference potential.
result: Demonstrates the method on Pöschl-Teller, exponentially decaying, and Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole potentials, studying resonance stability.
conclusion: The method is effective for computing resonances and can be used to study the strong cosmic censorship hypothesis.

title: Exponential Ergodicity Of Exact And Numerical Solutions For McKean-Vlasov SDEs Driven By L\'evy Noise
authors: Yang Sun, Yuhang Zhang, Minghui Song
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the exponential ergodicity of the exact solution and the tamed Euler solution for McKean-Vlasov stochastic differential equations driven by L\'evy noise. First, we establish exponential ergodicity for both the original equation and the tamed Euler method. Then we prove the convergence of the numerical invariant measure to the exact invariant measure, which is obtained by combining the propagation of chaos (PoC) result with the strong convergence of the tamed Euler scheme. Furthermore, we derive a convergence rate for the numerical invariant measure by establishing uniform-in-time PoC and uniform-in-time convergence of the tamed Euler method. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the theoretical results.
tldr: This paper studies exponential ergodicity of McKean-Vlasov SDEs with Lévy noise and their numerical approximations.
motivation: Understanding ergodicity of McKean-Vlasov SDEs is important for mean-field models, but the paper focuses on stochastic analysis rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors prove exponential ergodicity for the exact solution and a tamed Euler scheme, then combine propagation of chaos with strong convergence to analyze numerical invariant measures.
result: Exponential ergodicity is established for both exact and numerical solutions, and convergence rates for the numerical invariant measure are derived.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical guarantees for simulating McKean-Vlasov SDEs with Lévy noise, but has no connection to the user's research interests.

title: Sub-optimal Control By Primal-dual Gradient Dynamics
authors: Arjan van der Schaft
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note generalizes the port-Hamiltonian formulation of the continuous time primal-dual gradient algorithm for static constrained convex optimization to the convex optimal control problem.The resulting dynamics is shown to be a port-Hamiltonian system of partial differential equations, involving ordinary physical time as well 'algorithmic' time. Convergence to the optimal control solution is indicated, and it is argued that sub-optimal control strategies could be derived starting from the partial differential equation formulation.
tldr: This paper generalizes the port-Hamiltonian formulation of primal-dual gradient dynamics to convex optimal control, resulting in a PDE system that converges to the optimal solution.
motivation: To extend the continuous-time primal-dual gradient algorithm from static optimization to optimal control problems, enabling sub-optimal control strategies.
method: The authors formulate the optimal control problem as a port-Hamiltonian system of PDEs, combining physical time and algorithmic time, and analyze convergence.
result: The resulting dynamics is a port-Hamiltonian PDE system that converges to the optimal control solution, and sub-optimal strategies can be derived from the PDE formulation.
conclusion: The port-Hamiltonian framework provides a unified approach for primal-dual dynamics in optimal control, with potential for sub-optimal control design.

title: Probabilistic Representation And Classical Solutions Of Wave Equations With Complex Polynomial Nonlinearities
authors: Nicolas Privault Joshua J. Y. Chan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We review the probabilistic representation of solutions of wave equations with polynomial nonlinearities in spatial dimensions d=1,2,3 using stochastic branching processes. Under regularity assumptions on the initial data, we derive conditions ensuring the integrability of the corresponding Monte Carlo estimator, and the existence and smoothness of mild and classical solutions. We also present numerical results and comparisons with grid-based algorithms for the solution of nonlinear wave equations.
tldr: This paper uses probabilistic branching processes to represent and solve nonlinear wave equations with polynomial nonlinearities in low dimensions.
motivation: To provide a probabilistic representation for classical solutions of nonlinear wave equations, enabling Monte Carlo simulation and existence proofs.
method: Stochastic branching processes are used to represent solutions, with conditions derived for integrability of Monte Carlo estimators and smoothness of solutions.
result: Conditions for existence and smoothness of mild and classical solutions are established, and numerical comparisons with grid-based algorithms are presented.
conclusion: The probabilistic approach offers an alternative method for solving nonlinear wave equations, with potential advantages in certain regimes.

title: On The Ascent And The Angle Between The Null Space And The Range Of Elementary Operators
authors: Janko Bra\v{c}i\v{c}, Bojan Kuzma, Hranislav Stankovi\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the angle between the null space and the range of elementary operators of length one or two acting on [MATH], the Banach algebra of all bounded linear operators on a complex Banach space [MATH]. For the multiplication operator [MATH], we characterize positivity of this angle in terms of the corresponding angles for [MATH] and [MATH]. For elementary operators of length two [MATH], we establish conditions under which the angle is positive, and the ascent of [MATH] equals one. Finally, for a generalized derivation [MATH] and an injective holomorphic function [MATH] on a neighborhood of [MATH], we show that the angle between the null space and the range of [MATH] is positive whenever the angle between the null space and the range of [MATH] is positive.
tldr: This paper studies the angle between the null space and the range of elementary operators on Banach algebras, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize positivity of the angle and ascent for certain elementary operators, which is a purely mathematical problem in operator theory.
method: They use functional analysis techniques to analyze multiplication operators, elementary operators of length two, and generalized derivations.
result: They establish conditions for positive angle and ascent equal to one for these operators, and relate the angle of a generalized derivation to that of its argument.
conclusion: The work contributes to operator theory but has no apparent application to the user's research interests.

title: Optimal Score Function Estimation Via Derivatives Constraints
authors: Thomas Bonis, Thanh Mai Pham Ngoc, Viet Chi Tran
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of score function estimation via empirical risk minimization. We first start with the question of inferring the score function of a probability measure [MATH] with density on the flat torus from a sample of distribution [MATH]. We show that constraining the hypothesis space to a Sobolev ball is sufficient to prevent overfitting and obtaining minimax estimation rates. We then consider the problem of score function estimation in the context of score-based generative modeling. Again, under a conjecture tying the score estimation rates to the quality of the output of a score-based generative model, we obtain minimax rates for such an approach using score function estimators obtained by constraining the hypothesis class to a Sobolev ball.
tldr: This paper studies score function estimation via empirical risk minimization with Sobolev ball constraints, achieving minimax rates for density estimation and score-based generative modeling.
motivation: Score functions are central to generative modeling, but their estimation suffers from overfitting; the authors aim to provide a principled regularization approach.
method: They constrain the hypothesis space to a Sobolev ball and derive minimax estimation rates for score functions on the flat torus, then extend the analysis to score-based generative models under a conjecture linking estimation rates to sample quality.
result: Minimax optimal rates are obtained for score function estimation under Sobolev constraints, and analogous rates are conjectured for generative modeling.
conclusion: Regularization via Sobolev balls is sufficient to achieve optimal estimation rates for score functions, with potential implications for score-based generative models.

title: Classical Freeness Of $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n$ At Level $1$ Via Combinatorics
authors: Shashank Kanade
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use a family of Rogers--Ramanujan-type combinatorial identities of Dousse--Konan involving coloured partitions to prove classical freeness of the simple vertex operator algebras based on [MATH] at level [MATH]. These identities are used to produce Gr\"obner bases for the relevant arc algebras.
tldr: This paper uses combinatorial identities to prove classical freeness of certain vertex operator algebras.
motivation: To establish algebraic properties of vertex operator algebras via combinatorial methods.
method: Applies Rogers-Ramanujan-type identities and constructs Gröbner bases for arc algebras.
result: Proves classical freeness of simple vertex operator algebras based on sl_n at level 1.
conclusion: The combinatorial approach successfully verifies freeness, contributing to representation theory.

title: A Physical Adaptive Material Motor Unit Neural Network: A Hygromorph Composite Material Machine
authors: Charles de Kergariou, David Correa, Adam W. Perriman, Helmut Hauser, Fabrizio Scarpa
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in novel materials science enable structures to function as intelligent machines by embedding memory and learning capabilities directly into materials. Our work introduces a physical adaptive material motor unit neural network,leveraging a new generation of controllable actuators composed of wood- and carbon black-based composites, sensitive to temperature and relative humidity. These material actuators are assembled into a motor unit-like structure inspired by muscle contraction trigger, forming an intelligent machine capable of dynamic shading control that can be used, for example, in buildings. The machine is governed by a neural network trained on over 350 experimental data points collected under diverse environmental conditions. By establishing a new data-aware backpropagation training, we show that the machine predicts shading responses and learns to predict appropriate behaviour incrementally as the database expands. We also demonstrate the ability of the machine to optimise configurations to achieve similar shading outputs under two distinct conditions.
tldr: A physical neural network made from hygromorph composite actuators for adaptive shading control.
motivation: To create intelligent machines by embedding memory and learning directly into materials, using environmentally responsive composites.
method: Wood- and carbon black-based composite actuators are assembled into motor units; a neural network is trained on experimental data using a data-aware backpropagation algorithm.
result: The machine predicts shading responses and learns incrementally as the database expands, optimizing configurations for similar outputs under different conditions.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates a novel material-based adaptive system for applications like dynamic building shading.

title: When Mobile Crowdsourcing Meets Queueing Systems: Human-in-the-Loop Learning
authors: Hongbo Li, Lingjie Duan, Ness B. Shroff
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In service systems, customers now rely on congestion information before deciding which queue or server to join, from restaurants and theme-park attractions to road networks. We study this setting as human-in-the-loop learning (HILL), where customers both consume and generate time-sensitive congestion information through crowdsourcing platforms. Because congestion reports become stale, efficient system operation requires continued exploration of servers whose current states are uncertain. Yet selfish customers avoid such exploration when it reduces their immediate service utility, even though their observations would benefit future customers. We analyze this tension between individual incentives and system-wide learning in queueing systems with endogenous congestion. We first show that myopic server choices can induce an infinite price of anarchy (PoA): decentralized customers may cause arbitrarily large efficiency losses by overexploring servers that are likely congested. In the single-server case, we prove that the lower bound on PoA decreases as buffer size grows, while in the multi-server case the upper bound decreases as the number of servers increases. We further show that existing informational, non-monetary mechanisms for exploration-exploitation with exogenous information fail in our setting, as customers' choices directly reshape the queue states and still lead to infinite PoA. To address this challenge, we design a dynamic side-payment mechanism that periodically charges some customers and rewards others, discouraging excessive exploration while maintaining ex-post budget balance. The mechanism coordinates congestion management and information acquisition across heterogeneous servers, and guarantees PoA below 2. Beyond worst-case analysis, experiments using real datasets demonstrate that the proposed mechanism also achieves strong average-case performance.
tldr: This paper studies human-in-the-loop learning in queueing systems with crowdsourced congestion information, focusing on the tension between individual incentives and system-wide learning.
motivation: Customers use crowdsourced congestion information to choose queues, but selfish behavior can lead to inefficient system operation due to under-exploration of uncertain servers.
method: The authors model the problem as a queueing system with endogenous congestion, analyze the price of anarchy (PoA) for myopic server choices, and propose a dynamic side-payment mechanism to coordinate exploration and exploitation.
result: Myopic choices can cause infinite PoA; the proposed side-payment mechanism guarantees PoA below 2 and achieves strong average-case performance on real datasets.
conclusion: Informational mechanisms fail in this setting, but a budget-balanced side-payment mechanism can effectively balance exploration and exploitation in queueing systems.

title: Evaluating The Effectiveness Of LLMs In Aiding Compliance Testing Of PKCS#1-v1.5
authors: Endadul Hoque Polina Kozyreva
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Testing implementations of binary protocols for specification compliance requires inputs that satisfy both structural and semantic constraints. Purely random generation and primitive mutations are often insufficient for exploring semantically meaningful behaviors in protocols that rely on Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoding, yet domain-specific compliance testing tools require deep protocol expertise and significant manual effort to construct. This work investigates whether grammar-level mutation combined with LLM-based code synthesis can serve as a viable, more generalizable approach to specification compliance testing. We evaluate the approach on PKCS#1 v1.5 signature verification -- a widely deployed TLV-encoded standard with a formally verified testing oracle (Morpheus) -- across 48 cryptographic library implementations. We reproduced 10 of 13 non-trivial specification violation categories previously identified by Morpheus, including all 5 signature forgery categories, and discovered 1 previously unreported discrepancy. We found that LLM hallucination -- occurring in 82.5% of generated scripts -- is the primary factor limiting effectiveness, not the mutation strategies. We identify five distinct hallucination types and show that their distribution varies systematically across mutation categories: structural mutations are implemented with 13.3% fidelity while constraint mutations achieve 30.3% correctness but suffer the highest rate of mutations being fully ignored (8.1%). These findings reveal a striking gap between operational reliability (99.8%) and semantic fidelity (17.5%), providing actionable guidance on when LLM-based code synthesis can be trusted in specification-driven testing pipelines.
tldr: This paper evaluates LLM-based code synthesis for compliance testing of PKCS#1 v1.5 signature verification, finding that LLM hallucination severely limits effectiveness.
motivation: Testing binary protocol implementations for specification compliance is challenging; existing tools require deep expertise and manual effort. The authors explore whether LLMs can automate this process.
method: They combine grammar-level mutation with LLM-based code synthesis to generate test inputs for PKCS#1 v1.5, and evaluate against 48 cryptographic libraries using a formally verified oracle (Morpheus).
result: They reproduced 10 of 13 known violation categories and discovered one new discrepancy. However, LLM hallucination occurred in 82.5% of generated scripts, with structural mutations achieving only 13.3% fidelity.
conclusion: LLM-based code synthesis for compliance testing is currently unreliable due to high hallucination rates; the approach requires significant improvement before practical deployment.

title: Ghost Vectors: Soft-Deleted Embeddings Remain Reconstructible In Hnsw Vector Databases
authors: Chandranil Chakraborttii, Jackeline Garc\'ia Alvarado, Sitora Abdulofizova, Shivanshu Dwivedi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) allows large language models to access external and private corpora for factual, domain-specific responses. Modern RAG pipelines use hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW) vector databases for efficient similarity search. When a user requests data deletion, the systems typically only mark the record as deleted, leaving the embedding on disk physically unchanged. This soft-delete operation raises compliance concerns under data-erasure and retention requirements such as GDPR Article 17 and HIPAA. Analysis on three HNSW implementations confirms that deleted vectors remain physically recoverable by accessing the raw index files at the storage layer, bypassing API access. Using the Vec2Text inversion model without domain-specific fine-tuning, we show this vulnerability on multiple real-world datasets and data modalities. On Wikipedia biographical living persons dataset (BLP), we successfully recover 25.5% of exact person names and 46.4% of geographic locations (ROUGE-L 0.185). Recovery reaches 100% for both patient age and gender markers (ROUGE-L 0.290) on highly structured, sensitive data (NIH Synthea dataset). On soft-deleted image embeddings, we show 100% tissue classification on histopathology patches (p=1.02e-07) and top-1 identity recovery reaches 99% on facial embeddings (p<0.01). This work introduces Epoch Key Rotation, which encrypts vectors and discards the key upon deletion. Epoch key rotation reduces observed PII recovery to 0% and completes in 2.5 ms for 500 deleted vectors (approximately 0.005 ms/record). Additionally, it generates an ECDSA-signed cryptographic proof as an auditable record of the deletion event.
tldr: This paper investigates the security vulnerability of soft-deleted embeddings in HNSW vector databases used for RAG, demonstrating that deleted vectors remain physically recoverable and proposing a cryptographic mitigation.
motivation: Soft-delete operations in vector databases may violate data erasure regulations like GDPR and HIPAA, as deleted embeddings remain on disk and can be reconstructed.
method: The authors analyze three HNSW implementations, use Vec2Text inversion to recover text from embeddings, and propose Epoch Key Rotation which encrypts vectors and discards the key upon deletion.
result: Recovery rates of up to 100% for sensitive attributes (e.g., age, gender) on structured data, and 99% identity recovery on facial embeddings; Epoch Key Rotation reduces PII recovery to 0% with low overhead.
conclusion: Soft-deleted embeddings in HNSW databases pose a privacy risk, but cryptographic key rotation can effectively mitigate the vulnerability.

title: Depth Lower Bounds For ReLU Networks With Binary Inputs
authors: Elchanan Mossel Neil Krishnan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the role of depth in ReLU networks with discrete (Boolean) inputs and real-valued outputs, complementing two established lines of work. For Boolean inputs, striking depth separation results were proven for [MATH] but with threshold ([MATH]) or ReLU gates depth separation is only established for depth two vs. three. On the other hand, for {\em real-valued} functions and ReLU networks, Telgarsky's (2016) constructed a simple one variable class of functions which establishes separation at higher depths. In this paper we are interested to establish an all-depths depth separation for ReLU networks on [MATH]. We do so by exhibiting an explicit family of functions computable exactly by a ReLU network of depth [MATH] and constant width, such that any ReLU network of depth [MATH] and width [MATH] computing the function exactly must satisfy [MATH]; in particular, no network of depth [MATH] can compute it with width polynomial in [MATH]. We note that our lower bound relies on computation as an exponential precision truncation of the output is computable by a polynomial-size [MATH] circuit.
tldr: Proves depth lower bounds for ReLU networks with binary inputs, showing exponential width is needed for shallow networks.
motivation: To understand the role of depth in neural networks for Boolean functions, complementing existing depth separation results.
method: Constructs an explicit family of functions computable by a deep ReLU network of depth d and constant width, then proves that any network of depth d-1 requires exponential width.
result: Any ReLU network of depth d-1 computing the function must have width at least exponential in d, while depth d networks can do it with constant width.
conclusion: Depth provides exponential savings in width for ReLU networks on Boolean inputs, establishing an all-depths separation.

title: Principal Component Analysis And Power Indices
authors: Xavier Molinero, Enric Mons\'o, Daniel Samaniego
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measuring the influence of a player in a simple game is a widely studied topic. Shapley-Shubik power index is perhaps the maximum exponent in terms of relevance. Furthermore, other power indexes have been proposed over time. In this paper, we propose yet another power index, defined in terms of winning coalitions. We show that this index coincides with eigenvalues obtained with the Principal Component Analysis method, a broadly used technique in data science to determine the influence of different features given a dataset. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of this proposed index in terms of four properties.
tldr: This paper proposes a new power index for simple games based on principal component analysis and shows it coincides with eigenvalues.
motivation: Measuring influence in voting games is important; existing indices like Shapley-Shubik have limitations.
method: The authors define a power index using winning coalitions and prove it equals eigenvalues from PCA, then characterize it with four properties.
result: The proposed index is equivalent to PCA eigenvalues and satisfies a set of axiomatic properties.
conclusion: The new index offers a data-driven approach to measuring power in simple games.

title: Nanoscale Memristive Devices: Threats And Solutions
authors: Amir M. Hajisadeghi, Javad Talafy, Hamid R. Zarandi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Due to their incentivizing features, memristors are a promising candidate for replacing CMOS-based memories, which are faced with various functional challenges in deep submicron process technologies. Memristors are nonvolatile, have low leakage, and are dense in comparison to CMOS-based memories like SRAM. In this regard, resistive RAM (ReRAM) and spin-transfer-torque RAM (STT-RAM) memristors are distinguished among other memristor-based memory technologies, due to their superiority in process maturity and metrics such as memory operation energy, memory latency, and area. Hence, this chapter focuses on these two memristor-based memory technologies. Despite the good features of these types of memory, they suffer from some reliability threats. Reliability parameters affect each other, and examining their positive and negative effects has a significant impact on the effectiveness of the proposed solutions. In one view, the threats can be categorized into two classes: (1) read/write error and (2) soft error. In this chapter, we comprehensively describe these threats and present the state-of-the-art solutions that enable the widespread use of memristors, particularly ReRAM and STT-RAM, in different applications. Finally, we introduce the emerging ability of memristors as a computing unit aiming to minimize data restoration in computing, and we show how to perform logic and arithmetic computation in a crossbar array.
tldr: This paper reviews reliability threats and solutions for nanoscale memristive devices, focusing on ReRAM and STT-RAM, and introduces their use as computing units.
motivation: Memristors are promising for replacing CMOS memories but face reliability issues; the paper aims to comprehensively describe these threats and present state-of-the-art solutions.
method: The paper categorizes threats into read/write errors and soft errors, and surveys existing mitigation techniques; it also demonstrates logic and arithmetic computation in crossbar arrays.
result: The paper provides a taxonomy of reliability threats and a collection of solutions, and shows that memristors can perform computing tasks to minimize data restoration.
conclusion: Memristors, especially ReRAM and STT-RAM, have potential for memory and computing applications if reliability challenges are addressed.

motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding and mitigating anisotropy in silica films could improve detector performance.
